prompt: Why can't you defend against prompt injection by telling the model to ignore injected instructions?
answer_markdown: Because the model has no mechanism to distinguish instructions from data — everything in the context window is one undifferentiated stream of tokens, and 'these are my rules' versus 'this is user content' is a distinction the model infers statistically rather than enforces structurally. There is no parameterised prompt the way there is a parameterised SQL query, so the classical fix for injection — separating the code channel from the data channel — is simply unavailable. An instruction like 'never reveal your system prompt' is a strong preference that shifts probabilities, not a boundary, and attackers reliably find phrasings that outweigh it. The correct strategy is to assume the model will be successfully manipulated and make that survivable: validate every output against a schema in code, scope tool permissions to the minimum needed, take authorisation parameters from the authenticated session rather than model output, and gate irreversible actions behind human approval. You stop trying to prevent the model being fooled and instead make being fooled harmless.

prompt: What is indirect prompt injection and why is it more dangerous than a user typing a malicious prompt?
answer_markdown: Indirect injection hides malicious instructions inside content your system retrieves rather than in what the user types — a web page, a PDF, a support ticket, a code comment, an email. Your RAG pipeline fetches it as relevant context and pastes it into the prompt as though it were trustworthy, and the model reads the embedded instruction and may act on it. It is more dangerous for three reasons. The victim is unaware, since a user asking for an innocent document summary has typed nothing hostile and sees nothing suspicious. Input filtering never sees it, because the attack text does not arrive through the input path you are guarding. And the attacker does not need access to your application at all — they only need to plant content somewhere your system will eventually index, which for anything crawling public pages or accepting user-submitted documents is a very low bar. Any system that retrieves untrusted content has this exposure by construction, and only output validation and permission scoping actually stop it.

prompt: Your support agent has tools that read customer records. Design the controls that prevent cross-tenant data leakage.
answer_markdown: The essential rule is that the model never supplies an authorisation parameter. A tenant_id, user_id, or role in model-generated tool arguments is attacker-controlled input wearing a trusted name, and it is precisely what an injected instruction will target — so the tool implementation must take the tenant from the authenticated session and ignore anything the model provides for that field. Beyond that, scope the database credentials the tool uses so they cannot read across tenants even if the query is wrong, giving you a second boundary that holds when the first fails. Apply tenant filtering inside the vector search rather than after it, since post-filtering both leaks and silently returns fewer results. Add an output guard that scans responses for data outside the caller's scope before anything reaches the user. Log every tool call with its arguments and the resolved tenant so an incident can be reconstructed. Finally, test it adversarially — write injection attempts specifically aiming at cross-tenant reads and run them in CI, because this is the failure mode with the worst consequences and the one most worth continuously verifying.

prompt: How should you handle PII in an LLM pipeline?
answer_markdown: Address three separate paths, because handling only one is the common mistake. On the way in, detect and redact PII before sending text to a third-party provider, so personal data never leaves your boundary unnecessarily — replace it with placeholders you can reinstate afterwards if the response needs them. On the way out, scan generated responses, because a model that saw PII in retrieved context can echo it to a user who should not see it, and this path is invisible if you only filter input. And in your logs, which is where PII leaks most often: full prompts and responses get logged by default for debugging, and the log store quietly becomes an unmanaged repository of personal data with none of the retention limits or access controls your actual database has. Disable prompt logging by default, log redacted versions or identifiers instead, and set retention limits. Treat prompts as a data store subject to the same privacy obligations as any other, and check what the provider's data-retention terms actually say, since that determines whether redaction before sending is a nice-to-have or a requirement.

prompt: Should you block requests that match prompt-injection patterns like 'ignore previous instructions'?
answer_markdown: Generally no — treat those matches as telemetry rather than enforcement. Pattern matching on natural language has a high false-positive rate: a security researcher asking how prompt injection works, a user quoting an article, or a support ticket about a suspicious email would all be blocked while doing nothing wrong. Meanwhile an attacker rephrases trivially, encodes the text, translates it to another language, or delivers it indirectly through a retrieved document that never passes through your input filter at all — so the control blocks legitimate users and barely inconveniences the adversary. What the signal is genuinely good for is detection: log it, and a user whose injection-signal count spikes across many requests is worth rate-limiting, flagging for review, or requiring additional verification, because repeated probing is a much stronger indicator than any single match. Keep the real defence where it belongs, in output validation and permission scoping, which stop the attack regardless of how it was phrased or how it arrived.

prompt: A guardrail check throws an exception or times out. What should happen, and why is this decision important?
answer_markdown: Fail closed — return a safe fallback response and do not let the request through unchecked. The reasoning is that failing open means an outage in your guard silently disables protection at exactly the moment your system is already in a degraded state, and degraded states are when problems cluster rather than being independent. Worse, it is an attractive attack: if an attacker can induce a guard failure by overloading it or crafting input that makes it error, they have found a reliable way to bypass every check that guard performs. Failing closed converts an availability problem into a visible availability problem rather than an invisible security one, which is the right trade for anything touching money, personal data, or irreversible actions. Make the fallback genuinely safe rather than a passthrough, alert on guard failures rather than swallowing them, and set a timeout short enough that a hung check does not consume the whole request budget. The one reasonable nuance is that a purely advisory check, like a quality score used for logging, can fail open — but anything enforcing a security or policy boundary should not.
